claim: 20-30% of colorectal cancers may arise from precursors with serrated glands.
source: While 20–30% of colorectal cancers (CRCs) may arise from precursors with serrated glands, only 8–10% of CRCs manifest serrated morphology at diagnosis.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a general estimate from the literature.

claim: Only 8-10% of CRCs manifest serrated morphology at diagnosis.
source: While 20–30% of colorectal cancers (CRCs) may arise from precursors with serrated glands, only 8–10% of CRCs manifest serrated morphology at diagnosis.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a general estimate from the literature.

claim: CDX2 loss or BRAF mutations were found in approximately 60% of 36 human serrated CRCs studied.
source: We studied 36 human serrated CRCs and found CDX2 loss or BRAF mutations in ~60% of cases and often together (p=0.04).
evidence: The study analyzed 36 human serrated CRCs and found this frequency.

claim: CDX2 loss and BRAF mutations often occur together in human serrated CRCs (p=0.04).
source: We studied 36 human serrated CRCs and found CDX2 loss or BRAF mutations in ~60% of cases and often together (p=0.04).
evidence: Statistical analysis showed significant co-occurrence with p=0.04.

claim: CDX2Null/BRAFV600E expression in adult mouse intestinal epithelium led to serrated morphology tumors including carcinomas.
source: CDX2Null/BRAFV600E expression in adult mouse intestinal epithelium led to serrated morphology tumors (including carcinomas) and BRAFV600E potently interacted with CDX2 silencing to alter gene expression.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the mouse model experiments.

claim: BRAFV600E potently interacted with CDX2 silencing to alter gene expression.
source: CDX2Null/BRAFV600E expression in adult mouse intestinal epithelium led to serrated morphology tumors (including carcinomas) and BRAFV600E potently interacted with CDX2 silencing to alter gene expression.
evidence: Gene expression analysis showed cooperative effects.

claim: CDX2Null/BRAFV600E-mutant epithelium expressed gastric markers like human serrated lesions.
source: Like human serrated lesions, CDX2Null/BRAFV600E-mutant epithelium expressed gastric markers.
evidence: Immunohistochemical analysis showed expression of gastric markers.

claim: Organoids from CDX2Null/BRAFV600E-mutant colon epithelium showed serrated features.
source: Organoids from CDX2Null/BRAFV600E–mutant colon epithelium showed serrated features, and partially recapitulated the gene expression pattern in mouse colon tissues.
evidence: Organoid culture experiments demonstrated serrated morphology.

claim: Organoids from CDX2Null/BRAFV600E-mutant colon epithelium partially recapitulated the gene expression pattern in mouse colon tissues.
source: Organoids from CDX2Null/BRAFV600E–mutant colon epithelium showed serrated features, and partially recapitulated the gene expression pattern in mouse colon tissues.
evidence: Gene expression analysis of organoids compared to tissues.

claim: Many CRCs likely arise via clonal outgrowth and evolution of an epithelial cell in an adenomatous precursor lesion via adenoma-carcinoma progression.
source: Many CRCs likely arise via clonal outgrowth and evolution of an epithelial cell or cells in an adenomatous precursor lesion via so-called adenoma-carcinoma progression (Fearon, 2011; Fearon and Vogelstein, 1990).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Upwards of 20-30% of CRCs may arise via an alternative pathway termed the 'serrated pathway'.
source: But, upwards of 20–30% of CRCs may arise via an alternative pathway, often termed the 'serrated pathway', to reflect the saw-tooth or serrated morphology of the epithelial glands in the presumptive benign precursor lesions (Bettington et al., 2013; Jass, 2007a; Langner, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Serrated benign lesions arising in the colon and rectum include hyperplastic polyps (HPPs), sessile serrated adenomas/polyps (SSAs/SSPs), and traditional serrated adenomas (TSAs).
source: Serrated benign lesions arising in the colon and rectum include hyperplastic polyps (HPPs), sessile serrated adenomas/polyps (SSAs/SSPs), and traditional serrated adenomas (TSAs) (Bettington et al., 2013; Langner, 2015).
evidence: This classification is supported by citations.

claim: HPPs comprise the vast majority of serrated benign lesions detected and are most often found in the distal colon and rectum.
source: HPPs comprise the vast majority of serrated benign lesions detected and are most often found in the distal colon and rectum (Bettington et al., 2013; Langner, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: SSAs/SSPs account for 5-20% of serrated benign lesions and arise more often in the proximal colon.
source: SSAs/SSPs account for 5–20% of serrated benign lesions and arise more often in the proximal colon (Bettington et al., 2013; Langner, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: TSAs account for only about 1% of serrated benign lesions and arise mostly in the distal colon and rectum.
source: TSAs account for only about 1% of serrated benign lesions and arise mostly in the distal colon and rectum (Bettington et al., 2013; Langner, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Some SSAs/SSPs and TSAs showing dysplasia have potential to progress to CRC.
source: Some SSAs/SSPs and TSAs, such as those showing dysplasia, have potential to progress to CRC (Bettington et al., 2013; Jass, 2007a; Langner, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: HPPs do not show dysplasia and have generally been assumed to have negligible malignant potential.
source: HPPs do not show dysplasia and have generally been assumed to have negligible malignant potential (Bettington et al., 2013; Langner, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: In rare patients who develop HPPs along with other serrated colon polyps or with multiple and large HPPs, the lifetime risk of CRC is elevated.
source: However, in rare patients who develop HPPs along with other serrated colon polyps or in other patients with multiple and large HPPs, the lifetime risk of CRC is elevated (Jass, 2007b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Recurrent somatic mutations in CRCs affect roughly two-dozen different genes.
source: Recurrent somatic mutations in CRCs affect roughly two-dozen different genes (Cancer Genome Atlas Network, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to TCGA data.

claim: Mutations in the APC and TP53 TSGs are found in about 80% and 60% of CRCs, respectively.
source: Mutations in the APC and TP53 TSGs are found in about 80% and 60% of CRCs, respectively (Cancer Genome Atlas Network, 2012; Fearon, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: KRAS and BRAF oncogenic mutations are seen in roughly 40% and 10% of CRCs, respectively, and are mutually exclusive in a given CRC.
source: KRAS and BRAF oncogenic mutations are seen in roughly 40% and 10% of CRCs, respectively, and are mutually exclusive in a given CRC (Cancer Genome Atlas Network, 2012; Fearon, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: KRAS mutations most often result in missense substitutions at glycine codons 12 or 13.
source: KRAS mutations most often result in missense substitutions at glycine codons 12 or 13, and BRAF mutations most often result in missense substitutions of glutamic acid (E) for valine (V) at codon 600 (V600E) (Cancer Genome Atlas Network, 2012; Fearon, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: BRAF mutations most often result in missense substitutions of glutamic acid (E) for valine (V) at codon 600 (V600E).
source: KRAS mutations most often result in missense substitutions at glycine codons 12 or 13, and BRAF mutations most often result in missense substitutions of glutamic acid (E) for valine (V) at codon 600 (V600E) (Cancer Genome Atlas Network, 2012; Fearon, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Somatic BRAF mutations and loss or reduction of CDX2 expression individually and concurrently have been associated with poor prognosis in CRC patients.
source: Somatic BRAF mutations and loss or reduction of expression of the CDX2 homeobox transcription factor individually and concurrently have been associated with poor prognosis in CRC patients (Bae et al., 2015; Clarke and Kopetz, 2015; Dalerba et al., 2016; Landau et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: BRAF mutations are found in 70-80% of SSAs/SSPs.
source: BRAF mutations are found in 70–80% of SSAs/SSPs, whereas KRAS mutations are rare in these tumors (Bettington et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: KRAS mutations are rare in SSAs/SSPs.
source: BRAF mutations are found in 70–80% of SSAs/SSPs, whereas KRAS mutations are rare in these tumors (Bettington et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: BRAF mutations are found in about 70% of proximal colon HPPs and/or microvesicular histology HPPs.
source: BRAF mutations are found in about 70% of proximal colon HPPs and/or microvesicular histology HPPs, whereas KRAS mutations are found in up to 50% of HPPs in the distal colon and rectum and in goblet cell-rich histology HPPs.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from the literature.

claim: KRAS mutations are found in up to 50% of HPPs in the distal colon and rectum and in goblet cell-rich histology HPPs.
source: BRAF mutations are found in about 70% of proximal colon HPPs and/or microvesicular histology HPPs, whereas KRAS mutations are found in up to 50% of HPPs in the distal colon and rectum and in goblet cell-rich histology HPPs.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from the literature.

claim: TSAs mostly have KRAS mutations.
source: TSAs mostly have KRAS mutations (Bettington et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: APC mutations are rare or absent in serrated benign lesions.
source: APC mutations are rare or absent in serrated benign lesions and are perhaps also less common in CRCs arising from a serrated precursor (Bettington et al., 2013; Langner, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: APC mutations are perhaps less common in CRCs arising from a serrated precursor.
source: APC mutations are rare or absent in serrated benign lesions and are perhaps also less common in CRCs arising from a serrated precursor (Bettington et al., 2013; Langner, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature and uses speculative language 'perhaps'.

claim: Serrated pathway CRCs are associated with CIMP-H with p16INK4A and/or MLH1 gene silencing.
source: Other molecular features suggested to be associated with serrated pathway CRCs include CpG island methylation phenotype high-frequency (CIMP-H) with p16INK4A and/or MLH1 gene silencing, with MLH1 silencing linked to the microsatellite instability-high (MSI-H) phenotype (Bettington et al., 2013; Jass, 2007a; Langner, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: MLH1 silencing is linked to the microsatellite instability-high (MSI-H) phenotype.
source: Other molecular features suggested to be associated with serrated pathway CRCs include CpG island methylation phenotype high-frequency (CIMP-H) with p16INK4A and/or MLH1 gene silencing, with MLH1 silencing linked to the microsatellite instability-high (MSI-H) phenotype (Bettington et al., 2013; Jass, 2007a; Langner, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Serrated pathway-type CRCs have been suggested to express gastric epithelium markers such as MUC2, MUC5AC, MUC6 and ANXA10.
source: Serrated pathway-type CRCs have also been suggested to express gastric epithelium markers, such as mucin 2 (MUC2), MUC5AC, MUC6 and annexin A10 (ANXA10) (Kim et al., 2015; Tsai et al., 2015; Walsh et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Only 8-10% of CRCs manifest definitive serrated morphologic features at diagnosis.
source: Although up to 20–30% of CRCs have been estimated to arise from benign serrated precursors (Bettington et al., 2013; Jass, 2007a; Langner, 2015), only 8–10% of CRCs manifest definitive serrated morphologic features at diagnosis, characterized by epithelial gland serration, intracellular and extracellular mucin, and absence of necrosis (Bettington et al., 2013; García-Solano et al., 2010; Mäkinen, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Serrated CRCs are characterized by epithelial gland serration, intracellular and extracellular mucin, and absence of necrosis.
source: Although up to 20–30% of CRCs have been estimated to arise from benign serrated precursors (Bettington et al., 2013; Jass, 2007a; Langner, 2015), only 8–10% of CRCs manifest definitive serrated morphologic features at diagnosis, characterized by epithelial gland serration, intracellular and extracellular mucin, and absence of necrosis (Bettington et al., 2013; García-Solano et al., 2010; Mäkinen, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: CRCs with serrated morphology are presumed to arise mostly from serrated precursor lesions.
source: CRCs with serrated morphology (hereafter referred to as 'serrated CRCs') are presumed to arise mostly from serrated precursor lesions (Bettington et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Definitive biomarkers are lacking to identify CRCs that arose from serrated precursors but lack serrated morphology at diagnosis.
source: Definitive biomarkers are lacking to identify the CRCs that arose from serrated precursors but lack serrated morphology at diagnosis.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in current knowledge.

claim: Clinicopathologic studies have suggested that serrated CRCs may pursue a more aggressive course than their conventional counterparts.
source: Importantly, clinicopathologic studies have suggested that serrated CRCs may pursue a more aggressive course than their conventional counterparts (García-Solano et al., 2011)
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Loss or marked reduction of CDX2 expression was found in 21 (58%) of 36 serrated CRCs studied.
source: We found loss or marked reduction of CDX2 expression in 21 (58%) tumors (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's analysis of 36 serrated CRCs, shown in Figure 1.

claim: Strong nuclear staining for p53 protein in neoplastic cells was found in 21 (58%) of 36 serrated CRCs, consistent with expression of a missense mutant p53 protein.
source: Frequent alterations in the 36 CRCs included strong nuclear staining for p53 protein in neoplastic cells in 21 (58%) of cases, consistent with expression of a missense mutant p53 protein, and BRAFT1799A missense mutation encoding BRAFV600E protein in 20 (56%) cases (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding from immunohistochemical analysis, shown in Figure 1.

claim: BRAFT1799A missense mutation encoding BRAFV600E protein was found in 20 (56%) of 36 serrated CRCs.
source: Frequent alterations in the 36 CRCs included strong nuclear staining for p53 protein in neoplastic cells in 21 (58%) of cases, consistent with expression of a missense mutant p53 protein, and BRAFT1799A missense mutation encoding BRAFV600E protein in 20 (56%) cases (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding from DNA sequencing analysis, shown in Figure 1.

claim: Strong nuclear β-catenin staining, reflecting potential Wnt pathway mutations, was found in 19 (53%) of 36 serrated CRCs.
source: Other changes seen included strong nuclear β-catenin staining, reflecting potential Wnt pathway mutations, in 19 (53%) cases; p16INK4a expression loss in 18 (50%) cases; the CIMP-H phenotype in 12 (33%) cases, with 8 of these 12 cases having lost p16INK4A expression; the MSI-H phenotype in 5 (14%) cases; MLH1 expression loss in 4 (11%) cases, all of which were MSI-H cases; and KRAS codon 12 or 13 mutation in 7 (19%) cases, all of which lacked BRAFT1799A mutations (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding from immunohistochemical analysis, shown in Figure 1.

claim: p16INK4a expression loss was found in 18 (50%) of 36 serrated CRCs.
source: Other changes seen included strong nuclear β-catenin staining, reflecting potential Wnt pathway mutations, in 19 (53%) cases; p16INK4a expression loss in 18 (50%) cases; the CIMP-H phenotype in 12 (33%) cases, with 8 of these 12 cases having lost p16INK4A expression; the MSI-H phenotype in 5 (14%) cases; MLH1 expression loss in 4 (11%) cases, all of which were MSI-H cases; and KRAS codon 12 or 13 mutation in 7 (19%) cases, all of which lacked BRAFT1799A mutations (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding from immunohistochemical analysis, shown in Figure 1.

claim: The CIMP-H phenotype was found in 12 (33%) of 36 serrated CRCs.
source: Other changes seen included strong nuclear β-catenin staining, reflecting potential Wnt pathway mutations, in 19 (53%) cases; p16INK4a expression loss in 18 (50%) cases; the CIMP-H phenotype in 12 (33%) cases, with 8 of these 12 cases having lost p16INK4A expression; the MSI-H phenotype in 5 (14%) cases; MLH1 expression loss in 4 (11%) cases, all of which were MSI-H cases; and KRAS codon 12 or 13 mutation in 7 (19%) cases, all of which lacked BRAFT1799A mutations (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding from molecular analysis, shown in Figure 1.

claim: 8 of 12 CIMP-H cases had lost p16INK4A expression.
source: Other changes seen included strong nuclear β-catenin staining, reflecting potential Wnt pathway mutations, in 19 (53%) cases; p16INK4a expression loss in 18 (50%) cases; the CIMP-H phenotype in 12 (33%) cases, with 8 of these 12 cases having lost p16INK4A expression; the MSI-H phenotype in 5 (14%) cases; MLH1 expression loss in 4 (11%) cases, all of which were MSI-H cases; and KRAS codon 12 or 13 mutation in 7 (19%) cases, all of which lacked BRAFT1799A mutations (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding from combined molecular and immunohistochemical analysis, shown in Figure 1.

claim: The MSI-H phenotype was found in 5 (14%) of 36 serrated CRCs.
source: Other changes seen included strong nuclear β-catenin staining, reflecting potential Wnt pathway mutations, in 19 (53%) cases; p16INK4a expression loss in 18 (50%) cases; the CIMP-H phenotype in 12 (33%) cases, with 8 of these 12 cases having lost p16INK4A expression; the MSI-H phenotype in 5 (14%) cases; MLH1 expression loss in 4 (11%) cases, all of which were MSI-H cases; and KRAS codon 12 or 13 mutation in 7 (19%) cases, all of which lacked BRAFT1799A mutations (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding from molecular analysis, shown in Figure 1.

claim: MLH1 expression loss was found in 4 (11%) of 36 serrated CRCs, all of which were MSI-H cases.
source: Other changes seen included strong nuclear β-catenin staining, reflecting potential Wnt pathway mutations, in 19 (53%) cases; p16INK4a expression loss in 18 (50%) cases; the CIMP-H phenotype in 12 (33%) cases, with 8 of these 12 cases having lost p16INK4A expression; the MSI-H phenotype in 5 (14%) cases; MLH1 expression loss in 4 (11%) cases, all of which were MSI-H cases; and KRAS codon 12 or 13 mutation in 7 (19%) cases, all of which lacked BRAFT1799A mutations (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding from combined immunohistochemical and molecular analysis, shown in Figure 1.

claim: KRAS codon 12 or 13 mutation was found in 7 (19%) of 36 serrated CRCs, all of which lacked BRAFT1799A mutations.
source: Other changes seen included strong nuclear β-catenin staining, reflecting potential Wnt pathway mutations, in 19 (53%) cases; p16INK4a expression loss in 18 (50%) cases; the CIMP-H phenotype in 12 (33%) cases, with 8 of these 12 cases having lost p16INK4A expression; the MSI-H phenotype in 5 (14%) cases; MLH1 expression loss in 4 (11%) cases, all of which were MSI-H cases; and KRAS codon 12 or 13 mutation in 7 (19%) cases, all of which lacked BRAFT1799A mutations (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding from DNA sequencing analysis, shown in Figure 1.

claim: CDX2 loss/reduction and BRAF mutations were seen concurrently in 15 (42%) of 36 serrated CRCs (p=0.04).
source: However, we did find that CDX2 loss/reduction and BRAF mutations were seen concurrently in 15 (42%) cases (p=0.04) (Table 1 and Figure 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding with statistical significance, shown in Table 1 and Figure 1.

claim: CIMP-H status was more commonly seen in CDX2-negative tumors (p=0.04).
source: Besides BRAF mutations, other features more commonly seen in CDX2-negative tumors were CIMP-H status (p=0.04); membranous staining for β-catenin throughout the tumor, including the invasive front, likely reflecting wild type status for Wnt pathway genes (e.g, APC and CTNNB1, encoding β-catenin) (p=0.05); and retention of p16INK4A expression (p=0.04) (Table 1 and Figure 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding with statistical significance, shown in Table 1 and Figure 1.

claim: Membranous staining for β-catenin throughout the tumor, including the invasive front, was more commonly seen in CDX2-negative tumors (p=0.05).
source: Besides BRAF mutations, other features more commonly seen in CDX2-negative tumors were CIMP-H status (p=0.04); membranous staining for β-catenin throughout the tumor, including the invasive front, likely reflecting wild type status for Wnt pathway genes (e.g, APC and CTNNB1, encoding β-catenin) (p=0.05); and retention of p16INK4A expression (p=0.04) (Table 1 and Figure 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding with statistical significance, shown in Table 1 and Figure 1.

claim: Membranous β-catenin staining likely reflects wild type status for Wnt pathway genes (e.g., APC and CTNNB1).
source: Besides BRAF mutations, other features more commonly seen in CDX2-negative tumors were CIMP-H status (p=0.04); membranous staining for β-catenin throughout the tumor, including the invasive front, likely reflecting wild type status for Wnt pathway genes (e.g, APC and CTNNB1, encoding β-catenin) (p=0.05); and retention of p16INK4A expression (p=0.04) (Table 1 and Figure 1).
evidence: This is an inference based on established knowledge about β-catenin localization.

claim: Retention of p16INK4A expression was more commonly seen in CDX2-negative tumors (p=0.04).
source: Besides BRAF mutations, other features more commonly seen in CDX2-negative tumors were CIMP-H status (p=0.04); membranous staining for β-catenin throughout the tumor, including the invasive front, likely reflecting wild type status for Wnt pathway genes (e.g, APC and CTNNB1, encoding β-catenin) (p=0.05); and retention of p16INK4A expression (p=0.04) (Table 1 and Figure 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding with statistical significance, shown in Table 1 and Figure 1.

claim: BRAF mutations were associated with membranous staining for β-catenin (p=0.003).
source: BRAF mutations in these cases were associated with membranous staining for β-catenin (p=0.003), CIMP-H status (p=0.004), and ANXA10 expression (p<0.0001) (Table 1 and Figure 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding with statistical significance, shown in Table 1 and Figure 1.

claim: BRAF mutations were associated with CIMP-H status (p=0.004).
source: BRAF mutations in these cases were associated with membranous staining for β-catenin (p=0.003), CIMP-H status (p=0.004), and ANXA10 expression (p<0.0001) (Table 1 and Figure 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding with statistical significance, shown in Table 1 and Figure 1.

claim: BRAF mutations were associated with ANXA10 expression (p<0.0001).
source: BRAF mutations in these cases were associated with membranous staining for β-catenin (p=0.003), CIMP-H status (p=0.004), and ANXA10 expression (p<0.0001) (Table 1 and Figure 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding with statistical significance, shown in Table 1 and Figure 1.

claim: All 7 KRAS-mutant CRCs were CDX2-positive and lacked ANXA10 or MUC5AC expression, except for MUC5AC expression in one KRAS-mutant case.
source: Interestingly, all 7 KRAS-mutant CRCs were CDX2-positive and lacked ANXA10 or MUC5AC expression, except for MUC5AC expression in one KRAS-mutant case (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's analysis, shown in Figure 1.

claim: The median survival of CDX2P-CreERT2 Cdx2fl/fl mice treated with TAM was greater than 480 days.
source: The median survival of CDX2P-CreERT2 Cdx2fl/fl mice treated with TAM to activate Cre function and inactivate both Cdx2fl alleles (Blij et al., 2012) in colon epithelium was greater than 480 days (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the mouse survival study, shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The median survival of CDX2P-CreERT2 BrafCA mice was greater than 480 days after TAM treatment.
source: The median survival of CDX2P-CreERT2 BrafCA mice was greater than 480 days after TAM treatment (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the mouse survival study, shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The median survival of CDX2P-CreERT2 Cdx2fl/fl BrafCA mice was 103 days after TAM treatment.
source: In marked contrast, the median survival of CDX2P-CreERT2 Cdx2fl/fl BrafCA mice was 103 days after TAM treatment to concurrently target the Cdx2fl/fl and BrafCA alleles (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the mouse survival study, shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The median survival of mice with simultaneous targeting of one Apcfl allele together with Cdx2fl and BrafCA alleles was 158 days.
source: The median survival of mice with simultaneous targeting of one Apcfl allele together with Cdx2fl and BrafCA alleles was 158 days, indicating that inactivation of one Apc allele did not enhance tumor aggressiveness compared to the phenotype seen in CDX2P-CreERT2 Cdx2fl/fl BrafCA mice (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the mouse survival study, shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Inactivation of one Apc allele did not enhance tumor aggressiveness compared to the phenotype seen in CDX2P-CreERT2 Cdx2fl/fl BrafCA mice.
source: The median survival of mice with simultaneous targeting of one Apcfl allele together with Cdx2fl and BrafCA alleles was 158 days, indicating that inactivation of one Apc allele did not enhance tumor aggressiveness compared to the phenotype seen in CDX2P-CreERT2 Cdx2fl/fl BrafCA mice (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of survival data, shown in Figure 2A.

claim: When TAM-treated CDX2P-CreERT2 Cdx2fl/fl BrafCA mice were moribund, all mice had at least one large protuberant tumor (>10 mm) or multiple polypoid lesions at the proximal colon-ileal-cecal junction.
source: When the TAM-treated CDX2P-CreERT2 Cdx2fl/fl BrafCA mice were moribund, all of the mice had at least one large protuberant tumor (>10 mm) or multiple polypoid lesions at the proximal colon-ileal-cecal junction and each mouse had 2–6 independent tumor lesions with size >2 mm (Figure 2B and Figure 2—source data 2).
evidence: This is a primary finding from macroscopic examination of mice, shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Each CDX2P-CreERT2 Cdx2fl/fl BrafCA mouse had 2-6 independent tumor lesions with size >2 mm.
source: When the TAM-treated CDX2P-CreERT2 Cdx2fl/fl BrafCA mice were moribund, all of the mice had at least one large protuberant tumor (>10 mm) or multiple polypoid lesions at the proximal colon-ileal-cecal junction and each mouse had 2–6 independent tumor lesions with size >2 mm (Figure 2B and Figure 2—source data 2).
evidence: This is a primary finding from macroscopic examination of mice, shown in Figure 2B.

claim: All tumors arising in CDX2P-CreERT2 Cdx2fl/fl BrafCA mice showed both serrated and mucin-rich histological components.
source: All the tumors arising in CDX2P-CreERT2 Cdx2fl/fl BrafCA mice showed both serrated and mucin-rich histological components (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a primary finding from histological examination, shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The serrated components had a distinct serrated architecture with irregular bifurcation of the glands, and cells with eosinophilic and abundant cytoplasm, and vesicular nuclei with prominent nucleoli.
source: The serrated components had a distinct serrated architecture with irregular bifurcation of the glands, and the cells in these glands have eosinophilic and abundant cytoplasm, and vesicular nuclei with prominent nucleoli (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a primary finding from histological examination, shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The serrated components of mouse tumors closely resemble features of human serrated morphology CRCs.
source: These characteristics closely resemble features of human serrated morphology CRCs.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of histological features.

claim: In the mucin-rich components, the glands were tubular or cystic, and lined by bland cuboidal and columnar cells containing abundant mucin.
source: In the mucin-rich components, the glands were tubular or cystic, and lined by bland cuboidal and columnar cells containing abundant mucin (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a primary finding from histological examination, shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The mucin-rich components had only inactivated both Cdx2fl alleles, whereas the serrated histology epithelium had both Cdx2fl alleles and the BrafCA allele targeted.
source: Using DNA samples isolated from the serrated or mucin-rich regions by laser-capture microdissection, we found the mucin-rich components had only inactivated both Cdx2fl alleles, whereas the serrated histology epithelium had both Cdx2fl alleles and the BrafCA allele targeted (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is a primary finding from genotyping analysis, shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: In seven TAM-treated CDX2P-CreERT2 Cdx2fl/fl BrafCA mice studied, from 17-50% of the tumor lesions showed evidence that the serrated glands had invaded into the submucosa, indicative of carcinoma.
source: In the seven TAM-treated CDX2P-CreERT2 Cdx2fl/fl BrafCA mice studied, from 17–50% of the tumor lesions showed evidence that the serrated glands had invaded into the submucosa, indicative of carcinoma (Figure 2D and Figure 2—source data 2).
evidence: This is a primary finding from histological examination, shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Combined TAM-mediated targeting of an Apcfl allele together with the Cdx2fl and BrafCA alleles in CDX2P-CreERT2 Cdx2fl/fl BrafCA Apcfl/+ mice did not alter the histology of the tumor lesions compared to those arising in CDX2P-CreERT2 Cdx2fl/fl BrafCA mice with intact Apc alleles.
source: We found that combined TAM-mediated targeting of an Apcflallele together with the Cdx2fl and BrafCA alleles in CDX2P-CreERT2 Cdx2fl/fl BrafCA Apcfl/+ mice did not alter the histology of the tumor lesions compared to those arising in CDX2P-CreERT2 Cdx2fl/fl BrafCAmice with intact Apc alleles (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is a primary finding from histological comparison, shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: No apparent selection for loss of the remaining wild type Apc allele was seen in tumors arising in CDX2P-CreERT2 Cdx2fl/fl BrafCA Apcfl/+ mice, as no β-catenin nuclear or cytoplasmic staining was seen in the tumor tissues studied.
source: Furthermore, we saw no apparent selection for loss of the remaining wild type Apc allele in tumors arising in CDX2P-CreERT2 Cdx2fl/fl BrafCAApcfl/+ mice, as no β-catenin nuclear or cytoplasmic staining was seen in the CDX2P-CreERT2 Cdx2fl/fl BrafCA Apcfl/+ mouse tumor tissues studied (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is a primary finding from immunohistochemical analysis, shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Concurrent Cdx2 silencing combined with BRAFV600E expression in mouse intestinal epithelium leads to premature death of the mice due to the development of intestinal tumors, including carcinomas.
source: Our findings indicate concurrent Cdx2 silencing combined with BRAFV600E expression in mouse intestinal epithelium leads to premature death of the mice, due to the development of intestinal tumors, including carcinomas, and the tumors recapitulate histological features of human serrated morphology CRCs.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the survival and tumor data presented.

claim: The tumors arising in CDX2P-CreERT2 Cdx2fl/fl BrafCA mice recapitulate histological features of human serrated morphology CRCs.
source: Our findings indicate concurrent Cdx2 silencing combined with BRAFV600E expression in mouse intestinal epithelium leads to premature death of the mice, due to the development of intestinal tumors, including carcinomas, and the tumors recapitulate histological features of human serrated morphology CRCs.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on histological comparison.

claim: ANXA10 expression was seen in the serrated components of the tumors arising in the TAM-treated CDX2P-CreERT2 Cdx2fl/fl BrafCA mice.
source: Akin to the situation in human serrated morphology CRCs with CDX2 loss and BRAFT1799A mutations (Figure 1), ANXA10 expression was seen in the serrated components of the tumors arising in the TAM-treated CDX2P-CreERT2 Cdx2fl/fl BrafCA mice (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a primary finding from immunohistochemical analysis, shown in Figure 3A.

claim: ANXA10 expression was not seen in any of the mucin-rich tumor components, where only Cdx2 inactivation was present and BRAFV600E expression was absent.
source: ANXA10 expression was not seen in any of the mucin-rich tumor components, where only Cdx2 inactivation was present and BRAFV600E expression was absent (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a primary finding from immunohistochemical analysis, shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Phospho-ERK expression, indicating MAPK activation, was detected only in the serrated components of tumors.
source: The BRAF protein functions as an upstream activator of mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) signaling, and similar to ANXA10 expression, phospho-ERK expression, indicating MAPK activation, was detected only in the serrated components of tumors (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a primary finding from immunohistochemical analysis, shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Membranous β-catenin staining, strong MUC5AC expression, and BrdU incorporation were found in the serrated components of the tumors in the CDX2P-CreERT2 Cdx2fl/fl BrafCA mice.
source: Similar to the infrequent nuclear or cytoplasmic β-catenin staining and strong MUC5AC expression seen in most CDX2-defective and BRAFV600E-mutant human serrated CRCs (Figure 1), we found membranous β-catenin staining, strong MUC5AC expression, and bromo-deoxyuridine (BrdU) incorporation (indicating DNA synthesis) in the serrated components of the tumors in the CDX2P-CreERT2 Cdx2fl/fl BrafCA mice (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a primary finding from immunohistochemical analysis, shown in Figure 3B.

claim: No evidence for p53 nuclear protein accumulation was seen in the serrated and/or invasive components of CDX2P-CreERT2 Cdx2fl/fl BrafCA mouse tumors.
source: No evidence for p53 nuclear protein accumulation was seen in the serrated and/or invasive components (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a primary finding from immunohistochemical analysis, shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The tumors arising in the TAM-treated CDX2P-CreERT2 Cdx2fl/fl BrafCA mice showed significantly higher levels of phospho-EGFR expression, compared to very low level of phospho-EGFR in Cdx2−/−-mutant, BrafV600E-mutant, or normal control mouse cecal epithelium.
source: Consistent with a previous study showing that EGFR activation was found in majority of CRC cell lines harboring BRAFV600E mutation (Prahallad et al., 2012), the tumors arising in the TAM-treated CDX2P-CreERT2 Cdx2fl/fl BrafCAmice showed significant higher levels of phospho-EGFR expression, compared to very low level of phospho-EGFR in Cdx2−/−-mutant, BrafV600E-mutant, or normal control mouse cecal epithelium (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a primary finding from immunohistochemical analysis, shown in Figure 4.

claim: All tumors from 5 CDX2P-CreERT2 Cdx2fl/fl BrafCA mice were MSS (microsatellite stable).
source: All tumors from 5 CDX2P-CreERT2 Cdx2fl/fl BrafCAmice were MSS, and we did not detect significant methylation at the p16Ink4a promoter in the tumors (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding from microsatellite analysis, shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: No significant methylation at the p16Ink4a promoter was detected in the tumors from CDX2P-CreERT2 Cdx2fl/fl BrafCA mice.
source: All tumors from 5 CDX2P-CreERT2 Cdx2fl/fl BrafCAmice were MSS, and we did not detect significant methylation at the p16Ink4a promoter in the tumors (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding from bisulfite sequencing analysis, shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Concurrent CDX2 and BRAFV600E defects are key instigating lesions in development of the serrated mouse tumors.
source: Overall, the findings suggest concurrent CDX2 and BRAFV600E defects are key instigating lesions in development of the serrated mouse tumors.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the molecular analysis data.

claim: The principal components analysis showed the Cdx2−/− BrafV600E mutant epithelium clearly had distinct global patterns of gene expression from that of normal colon epithelium or mutant colon epithelium of the single mutant genotypes.
source: The principal components analysis showed the Cdx2−/− BrafV600E mutant epithelium clearly had distinct global patterns of gene expression from that of normal colon epithelium or mutant colon epithelium of the single mutant genotypes (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a primary finding from gene expression analysis, shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Combined Cdx2 inactivation and BrafV600E activation had very strong cooperative interactions in altering the expression of a large number of genes.
source: The gene expression patterns in Cdx2−/−BrafV600E-mutant epithelium indicated that combined Cdx2 inactivation and BrafV600E activation had very strong cooperative interactions in altering the expression of a large number of genes, with many genes dramatically activated in expression and a smaller collection of genes dramatically down-regulated (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a primary finding from gene expression analysis, shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Anxa10 was the top activated gene in the Cdx2−/− BrafV600E-mutant epithelium.
source: Interestingly, notwithstanding the data above showing that the ANXA10 protein was strongly expressed in human serrated morphology CRC and mouse Cdx2−/− BrafV600E serrated tumor epithelium, it was still a surprise that Anxa10 was the top activated gene in the Cdx2−/− BrafV600E-mutant epithelium (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a primary finding from gene expression analysis, shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Cdx2 loss or BrafV600E expression alone had only modest effect on Anxa10 expression relative to levels in control epithelium, whereas concurrent Cdx2 and BrafV600E defects led to a roughly 100-fold activation of Anxa10.
source: Cdx2 loss or BrafV600E expression alone had only modest effect on Anxa10 expression relative to levels in control epithelium, whereas concurrent Cdx2 and BrafV600E defects led to a roughly 100-fold activation of Anxa10 (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a primary finding from gene expression analysis, shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The Pla2g2a gene was a non-induced gene in Cdx2−/− BrafV600E-mutant epithelium compared to its induction in Cdx2−/− mutant, BrafV600E-mutant, or Apc-mutant epithelium.
source: Interestingly, the Pla2g2a gene, which encodes a secretory phospholipase A2 protein and which is also known as Mom-1 (modifier of multiple intestinal neoplasia 1) for its defined role as a potent genetic modifier of the ApcMin intestinal neoplasia phenotype (Cormier et al., 1997), was a non-induced gene in Cdx2−/− BrafV600E -mutant epithelium compared to its induction in Cdx2−/− mutant, BrafV600E-mutant, or Apc-mutant epithelium (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a primary finding from gene expression analysis, shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The top pathways for activated gene expression patterns in the Cdx2−/− BrafV600E-mutant epithelium were epithelial-mesenchymal transition, KRAS signaling, and hypoxia.
source: The top pathways for activated gene expression patterns in the Cdx2−/− BrafV600E-mutant epithelium were epithelial-mesenchymal transition, KRAS signaling, and hypoxia, and the top pathways for down-regulated gene expression were cholesterol homeostasis, adipogenesis, and xenobiotic metabolism (Table 2).
evidence: This is a primary finding from pathway enrichment analysis, shown in Table 2.

claim: The top pathways for down-regulated gene expression in the Cdx2−/− BrafV600E-mutant epithelium were cholesterol homeostasis, adipogenesis, and xenobiotic metabolism.
source: The top pathways for activated gene expression patterns in the Cdx2−/− BrafV600E-mutant epithelium were epithelial-mesenchymal transition, KRAS signaling, and hypoxia, and the top pathways for down-regulated gene expression were cholesterol homeostasis, adipogenesis, and xenobiotic metabolism (Table 2).
evidence: This is a primary finding from pathway enrichment analysis, shown in Table 2.

claim: Strong association was observed between mouse gene expression data and human CRC data with significant enrichment of genes found 'up' in both data-sets as well as 'down' in both data-sets (p=4.5×10−49).
source: We observed strong association between our mouse data and human CRC data with significant enrichment of genes found 'up' in both data-sets as well as 'down' in both data-sets, and few disagreements between both data-sets (p=4.5×10−49, Mantel-Haenszel Chi-Square test of association) (Figure 5 and Figure 5—source data 2).
evidence: This is a primary finding from comparative gene expression analysis.

claim: The genes that showed strong cooperative interaction between Cdx2 loss and BrafV600E expression in the mouse colon tumors were found to be significantly enriched in human serrated CRCs vs. conventional CRCs (p=1.4×10−11).
source: Again, the genes that showed strong cooperative interaction between Cdx2 loss and BrafV600E expression in the mouse colon tumors (either up or down) were found to be significantly enriched in human serrated CRCs vs. conventional CRCs (p=1.4×10−11) (Figure 5—source data 2).
evidence: This is a primary finding from comparative gene expression analysis using Finnish data.

claim: The gene signature found in the Cdx2-/-/BrafV600E mouse model is highly instructive to identify the serrated subset of human CRCs.
source: Our findings suggested that the gene signature found in our Cdx2-/-/BrafV600E mouse model is highly instructive to identify the serrated subset of human CRCs.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the comparative gene expression analysis.

claim: In normal mouse gastro-intestinal tissues studied, only gastric antrum epithelium and duodenum epithelium showed positive staining for PDX1, with no staining in epithelium from terminal ileum, cecum, colon and rectum.
source: In the normal mouse gastro-intestinal tissues studied, only gastric antrum epithelium and duodenum epithelium showed positive staining for PDX1, with no staining in epithelium from terminal ileum, cecum, colon and rectum (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding from immunohistochemical analysis, shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Strong PDX1 staining was seen in colon epithelium from CDX2P-CreERT2 Cdx2fl/fl BrafCA mice.
source: In contrast, strong PDX1 staining was seen in colon epithelium from CDX2P-CreERT2 Cdx2fl/fl BrafCA mice (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a primary finding from immunohistochemical analysis, shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Strong and diffuse PDX1 staining was also seen in colon epithelium of CDX2P-CreERT2 Cdx2fl/fl mice.
source: Strong and diffuse PDX1 staining was also seen in colon epithelium of CDX2P-CreERT2 Cdx2fl/fl mice (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding from immunohistochemical analysis, shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Activation of PDX1 expression was seen in colon epithelium of CDX2P-CreERT2 Cdx2fl/fl mice as early as 7 days after TAM injection to target the Cdx2 alleles.
source: Activation of PDX1 expression was seen in colon epithelium of CDX2P-CreERT2 Cdx2fl/fl mice as early as 7 days after TAM injection to target the Cdx2 alleles (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding from immunohistochemical analysis, shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Strong PDX1 expression was seen in the majority of neoplastic cells in the tumors arising in the CDX2P-CreERT2 Cdx2fl/fl BrafCA mice.
source: While strong PDX1 expression was seen in the majority of neoplastic cells in the tumors arising in the CDX2P-CreERT2 Cdx2fl/fl BrafCA mice (Figure 6A), PDX1 expression was largely restricted to apical region epithelial cells in colon epithelium of CDX2P-CreERT2 Cdx2fl/fl mice (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding from immunohistochemical analysis, shown in Figure 6A.

claim: PDX1 expression was largely restricted to apical region epithelial cells in colon epithelium of CDX2P-CreERT2 Cdx2fl/fl mice.
source: While strong PDX1 expression was seen in the majority of neoplastic cells in the tumors arising in the CDX2P-CreERT2 Cdx2fl/fl BrafCA mice (Figure 6A), PDX1 expression was largely restricted to apical region epithelial cells in colon epithelium of CDX2P-CreERT2 Cdx2fl/fl mice (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding from immunohistochemical analysis, shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: 30 (83.3%) of 36 serrated morphology human CRC cases had strong PDX1 expression, including all 26 of the cases with CDX2 loss/reduction and/or BRAFT1799A mutations.
source: We then assessed the 36 serrated morphology human CRC cases, finding that 30 (83.3%) had strong PDX1 expression, including all 26 of the cases with CDX2 loss/reduction and/or BRAFT1799A mutations (Figure 1 and Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a primary finding from immunohistochemical analysis of human samples, shown in Figure 1 and Figure 6B.

claim: CDX2 expression was retained in all goblet cell-rich histology HPPs.
source: While CDX2 expression was retained in all goblet cell-rich histology HPPs, all 20 of the other benign serrated lesions studied had greatly reduced or absent CDX2 expression (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is a primary finding from immunohistochemical analysis of benign serrated lesions, shown in Figure 6C.

claim: All 20 of the benign serrated lesions studied (excluding goblet cell-rich HPPs) had greatly reduced or absent CDX2 expression.
source: While CDX2 expression was retained in all goblet cell-rich histology HPPs, all 20 of the other benign serrated lesions studied had greatly reduced or absent CDX2 expression (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is a primary finding from immunohistochemical analysis of benign serrated lesions, shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Induction of PDX1 expression was seen in all benign serrated lesion types and in all 24 benign lesions studied.
source: Moreover, induction of PDX1 expression was seen in all benign serrated lesion types (Figure 6C) and in all 24 benign lesions studied.
evidence: This is a primary finding from immunohistochemical analysis of benign serrated lesions, shown in Figure 6C.

claim: PDX1 was expressed in 132 (33%) of 395 CRCs not selected for any specific morphologic features.
source: We found PDX1 was expressed in 132 (33%) of the 395 CRCs studied (Figure 6—source data 1), a percentage which is curiously not far from the upper estimate that 30% of CRCs may arise through a serrated pathway.
evidence: This is a primary finding from immunohistochemical analysis of a large CRC cohort.

claim: Strong staining for CDX2 was seen in 287 (73%) of 395 CRCs, with reduced but detectable CDX2 staining in 73 (18%) and loss of CDX2 expression in 35 (9%).
source: Strong staining for CDX2 was seen in 287 (73%) of the 395 CRCs, with reduced but detectable CDX2 staining in 73 (18%) of the 395 cases and loss of CDX2 expression in 35 (9%) of the 395 cases (Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding from immunohistochemical analysis of a large CRC cohort.

claim: ANXA10 expression was seen in 24 (67%) of the 36 human serrated CRCs.
source: ANXA10 expression, which was seen in 24 (67%) of the 36 human serrated CRCs, was only expressed in 26 (7%) of the 395 CRCs.
evidence: This is a primary finding from immunohistochemical analysis.

claim: ANXA10 was only expressed in 26 (7%) of 395 CRCs not selected for morphologic features.
source: ANXA10 expression, which was seen in 24 (67%) of the 36 human serrated CRCs, was only expressed in 26 (7%) of the 395 CRCs.
evidence: This is a primary finding from immunohistochemical analysis of a large CRC cohort.

claim: Normal mouse colon epithelium-derived organoids formed uniform glandular structures in the presence of media supplemented with Wnt3a, R-spondin, noggin, EGF, and HGF.
source: Normal mouse colon epithelium-derived organoids formed uniform glandular structures in the presence of media supplemented with Wnt3a, R-spondin, noggin, epidermal growth factor (EGF), and hepatocyte growth factor (HGF) (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a primary finding from organoid culture experiments, shown in Figure 7.

claim: The cells in the normal epithelium-derived organoids lacked dysplasia and resembled normal columnar colon epithelial cells.
source: The cells in the normal epithelium-derived organoids lacked dysplasia and resembled normal columnar colon epithelial cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding from histological examination of organoids.

claim: Apc-mutant (Apc−/−) mouse colon epithelium formed organoids in the absence of Wnt3a and R-spondin supplementation.
source: Apc-mutant (Apc−/−) mouse colon epithelium formed organoids in the absence of Wnt3a and R-spondin supplementation, as expected for cells with bi-allelic Apc mutations and constitutive activation of β-catenin/TCF transcription.
evidence: This is a primary finding from organoid culture experiments.

claim: The Apc−/− epithelium-derived organoids were larger than normal epithelium-derived organoids, and the cells showed dysplasia.
source: The Apc−/− epithelium-derived organoids were larger than normal epithelium-derived organoids, and the cells showed dysplasia, with larger and more irregularly shaped nuclei containing open chromatin and a loss of the normal basal polarity of the nuclei (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a primary finding from histological examination of organoids, shown in Figure 7.

claim: Organoids derived from Cdx2Null mouse colon epithelium showed minimal if any alterations in morphology relative to organoids derived from normal colon epithelium.
source: Organoids derived from Cdx2Null mouse colon epithelium were grown in the presence of the full growth factor supplementation, and the organoids showed minimal if any alterations in morphology relative to organoids derived from normal colon epithelium (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a primary finding from organoid culture experiments, shown in Figure 7.

claim: Organoids derived from CDX2Null/BRAFV600E-mutant epithelium could be grown without EGF supplementation of the media.
source: Organoids derived from CDX2Null/BRAFV600E-mutant epithelium could be grown without EGF supplementation of the media, due presumably to constitutive BRAF→MEK1/2→ERK1/2 MAP kinase signaling driven by the BRAFV600E oncoprotein kinase.
evidence: This is a primary finding from organoid culture experiments.

claim: Initially, roughly 25% of the organoids derived from the CDX2Null/BRAFV600E-mutant epithelium showed serrated glandular structures.
source: Initially, roughly 25% of the organoids derived from the CDX2Null/BRAFV600E-mutant epithelium showed serrated glandular structures, with invaginations of epithelial cells into the organoid lumen, and epithelial cells with eosinophilic or clear and abundant cytoplasm, vesicular nuclei with distinct nucleoli, and loss of basal polarity of the cells, closely resembling mouse and human epithelium with serrated morphology (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a primary finding from organoid culture experiments, shown in Figure 7.

claim: CDX2 expression was seen in all organoids where Cdx2 gene function remained intact.
source: CDX2 expression was seen in all organoids where Cdx2 gene function remained intact (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a primary finding from immunohistochemical analysis of organoids, shown in Figure 7.

claim: Strong and homogeneous PDX1 expression was found only in the CDX2Null/BRAFV600E-mutant epithelium.
source: Strong and homogeneous PDX1 expression was found only in the CDX2Null/BRAFV600E-mutant epithelium.
evidence: This is a primary finding from immunohistochemical analysis of organoids.

claim: After three-four in vitro passages of the CDX2Null/BRAFV600E-mutant organoids, a significant decrease in the percentage of organoids displaying serrated morphology was observed.
source: After three-four in vitro passages of the CDX2Null/BRAFV600E-mutant organoids, we observed a significant decrease in the percentage of organoids displaying serrated morphology, suggesting that serrated morphologic appearance as a phenotypic trait may not be stable in some neoplastic cell populations over time.
evidence: This is a primary finding from organoid culture experiments.

claim: Serrated morphologic appearance as a phenotypic trait may not be stable in some neoplastic cell populations over time.
source: After three-four in vitro passages of the CDX2Null/BRAFV600E-mutant organoids, we observed a significant decrease in the percentage of organoids displaying serrated morphology, suggesting that serrated morphologic appearance as a phenotypic trait may not be stable in some neoplastic cell populations over time.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of decreased serrated morphology over passages.

claim: Only 4 out of 20 genes up-regulated in the in vivo setting showed significant cooperative interaction between CDX2 silencing and BRAFV600E expression in the organoid model system (Npy, Gkn2, Ivl and Tmprss11e).
source: Interestingly, only 4 out of the 20 genes up-regulated in the in vivo setting (i.e., Npy, Gkn2, Ivl and Tmprss11e) showed significant cooperative interaction between CDX2 silencing and BRAFV600E expression in the organoid model system (Figure 8A and C).
evidence: This is a primary finding from gene expression analysis of organoids, shown in Figure 8A and C.

claim: Lower expression of Anxa10 was found in the CDX2Null/BRAFV600E-mutant organoids compared to the normal control or BrafVE organoids.
source: Lower expression of Anxa10 was found in the CDX2Null/BRAFV600E-mutant organoids compared to the normal control or BrafVE organoids (Figure 8A and C).
evidence: This is a primary finding from gene expression analysis of organoids, shown in Figure 8A and C.

claim: The expression of Npy, Gkn2, Ivl and Tmprss11e as well as Anxa10 in CDX2Null/BRAFV600E-mutant organoids was markedly inhibited by MEK1/2-inhibitor (AZD6244) treatment.
source: The expression of Npy, Gkn2, Ivl and Tmprss11e as well as Anxa10 in CDX2Null/BRAFV600E-mutant organoids was markedly inhibited by MEK1/2-inhibitor (AZD6244) treatment.
evidence: This is a primary finding from gene expression analysis of drug-treated organoids.

claim: The effectiveness of AZD6244 treatment was verified by its inhibitory effect on expression of MAPK target genes, Dusp6 and Fos, in all the organoids treated.
source: The effectiveness of AZD6244 treatment was verified by its inhibitory effect on expression of MAPK target genes, Dusp6 and Fos, in all the organoids treated (Figure 8B and C) and was also confirmed by its ability to significantly reduce the level of phospho-ERK (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding from gene expression and immunohistochemical analysis, shown in Figure 8B, C and Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: 17 of the 36 serrated morphology CRCs studied were rectal lesions and four were distal colon lesions, with only 15 of the 36 serrated morphology CRCs arising in the proximal colon.
source: However, in contrast to the notion that CRCs arising from serrated precursors are nearly always or even predominantly right-sided lesions with CIMP-H and MSI-H phenotypes, 17 of the 36 serrated morphology CRCs that we studied were rectal lesions and four were distal colon lesions, with only 15 of the 36 serrated morphology CRCs arising in the proximal colon.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's analysis of tumor location.

claim: The CIMP-H phenotype was observed more frequently in the human serrated morphology CRCs with CDX2 loss and BRAFT1799A mutations (10 of 15 such cases) than in the CRCs lacking concurrent CDX2 loss and BRAFT1799A mutations (3 of 21 such cases).
source: We did observe the CIMP-H phenotype more frequently in the human serrated morphology CRCs with CDX2 loss and BRAFT1799A mutations (i.e., CIMP-H in 10 of 15 such cases) than in the CRCs lacking concurrent CDX2 loss and BRAFT1799Amutations (i.e., CIMP-H in only 3 of 21 such cases).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's molecular analysis.

claim: The 10 CIMP-H cases with concurrent CDX2 loss and BRAFT1799A mutation included four cases arising in the rectum and only 2 of 10 CIMP-H cases displayed the MSI-H phenotype and had lost MLH-1 protein expression.
source: However, our 10 CIMP-H cases with concurrent CDX2 loss and BRAFT1799A mutation included four cases arising in the rectum and only 2 of 10 CIMP-H cases displayed the MSI-H phenotype and had lost MLH-1 protein expression.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's molecular and pathological analysis.

claim: A potentially significant fraction of serrated morphology CRCs may arise from precursor lesions other than proximal colon SSAs/SSPs.
source: Hence, our data imply that a potentially significant fraction of serrated morphology CRCs may arise from precursor lesions other than proximal colon SSAs/SSPs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the location and molecular features of the serrated CRCs studied.

claim: While CDX2-null/low and BRAFV600E-mutant serrated morphology CRCs often manifested the CIMP-H phenotype, most serrated morphology CRCs lacking concurrent CDX2 and BRAFV600E defects did not manifest the CIMP-H phenotype.
source: Also, while CDX2-null/low and BRAFV600E-mutant serrated morphology CRCs often manifested the CIMP-H phenotype, most serrated morphology CRCs lacking concurrent CDX2 and BRAFV600E defects did not manifest the CIMP-H phenotype.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's molecular analysis.

claim: The MSI-H phenotype was not significantly enriched in the 36 serrated morphology CRCs as a group (5 of 36 cases – 14%) relative to the established prevalence of 15% in CRCs in general.
source: In addition, the MSI-H phenotype was not significantly enriched in our 36 serrated morphology CRCs as a group (5 of 36 cases – 14%) relative to the established prevalence of 15% in CRCs in general (Bettington et al., 2013; Cancer Genome Atlas Network, 2012; Fearon, 2011).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's molecular analysis compared to literature.

claim: A prior study reported that the MSI-H phenotype was only seen in 16% of serrated morphology CRCs.
source: Consistent with our findings, a prior study reported that the MSI-H phenotype was only seen in 16% of serrated morphology CRCs (García-Solano et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: The mouse model described is the first serrated mouse colon cancer model based on two signature defects common to a significant subset of human serrated morphology CRCs.
source: The mouse model of serrated intestinal tumorigenesis, including carcinomas, that we describe here, based on concurrent Cdx2 inactivation and BRAFV600E expression in distal mouse intestinal epithelium, is the first serrated mouse colon cancer model to our knowledge to be based on two signature defects common to a significant subset of human serrated morphology CRCs.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the model.

claim: Prior serrated tumorigenesis models using conditional activation of a mutant Kras allele in the mouse intestinal tract together with concurrent p16Ink4a/Arf or Pten TSG inactivation can promote outgrowth of dysplastic lesions and occasionally progression of some lesions to carcinoma.
source: Prior serrated tumorigenesis models using conditional activation of a mutant Kras allele in the mouse intestinal tract together with concurrent p16Ink4a/Arf or Pten TSG inactivation(Bennecke et al., 2010; Davies et al., 2014), can promote outgrowth of dysplastic lesions and occasionally progression of some lesions to carcinoma.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Only seven of the 36 (20%) serrated morphology CRCs studied had KRAS mutations and only two of the seven KRAS-mutant serrated CRCs had lost p16INK4A expression.
source: However, our data suggest potentially uncertain relevance of Kras-mutation-based mouse models with respect to serrated morphology human CRCs, as only seven of the 36 (20%) serrated morphology CRCs that we studied had KRAS mutations and only two of the seven KRAS-mutant serrated CRCs had lost p16INK4A expression.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's molecular analysis.

claim: The low overall frequency of PTEN mutations in human primary CRCs raises questions about the relevance of mouse models combining Kras activation and Pten inactivation to model serrated CRC.
source: Besides the modest-moderate frequency of KRAS mutations in human serrated CRCs, the low overall frequency of PTEN mutations in human primary CRCs raises some questions about the relevance of mouse models combining Kras activation and Pten inactivation to model serrated CRC.
evidence: This is an inference based on the frequency of PTEN mutations in human CRCs.

claim: A prior mouse model where BrafV600E conditional activation in small intestine in concert with p16Ink4a inactivation led to tumors with some serrated morphological features.
source: A prior mouse model has been reported where BrafV600E conditional activation in small intestine in concert with p16Ink4a inactivation led to tumors with some serrated morphological features(Carragher et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: The prior BRAFV600E-expressing and p16Ink4a mutant mouse model developed tumors in many tissues besides the intestinal tract (e.g., liver, lung, stomach), limiting its utility.
source: While p16INK4A expression loss is common in BRAFV600E-mutant human serrated CRCs, the prior BRAFV600E-expressing and p16Ink4amutant mouse model developed tumors in many tissues besides the intestinal tract (e.g., liver, lung, stomach), limiting its utility.
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Rad et al showed that activation of BrafV600E specifically in mouse intestinal tissues instigated hyperplasia and dysplasia with serrated features, and a very small subset of the tumors progressed over time to invasive carcinomas.
